body_html:
The best apps to learn Spanish are not interchangeable. Each one is good at one thing, whether that is habit, grammar, listening, speaking or vocabulary, and weak at others. I have used every app on this list over the years, some for months, and the biggest lesson I learned is that no single app will make you fluent. The learners who progress fastest combine two or three apps that cover different skills. Here is what each app is really good for, where it falls short and how I would combine them.

Quick answer
  • Best for building a daily habit: Duolingo
  • Best for structured grammar: Babbel
  • Best for speaking and pronunciation: Pimsleur
  • Best for listening: Dreaming Spanish
  • Best free course: Language Transfer
  • Best for real conversation: a tutor on italki or Preply
{{toc}}

Apps for structure and daily practice

1. Duolingo

Best for: building a daily habit and learning the basics · Level: A1–B2

Duolingo’s real strength is motivation. The streaks, short lessons and reminders make it easy to do something every day, and that consistency matters more than any method. In 2026 its free content was extended to more advanced levels, with stories for reading and audio lessons for listening. I still think it is the easiest way to start.

Where it falls short: it explains little grammar, and you can collect a long streak while still being unable to hold a conversation. Use it as a warm-up, not as your whole plan.

Get it on the App Store → · duolingo.com

2. Babbel

Best for: learners who want grammar explained and real-life dialogues · Level: A1–B2

Babbel feels more like a course than a game. Lessons are built around realistic conversations, and grammar is explained as you go, so you understand why something is said a certain way. For adults who want structure without a textbook, it is one of the most balanced options.

Where it falls short: it is paid, and like any app it can’t replace speaking with real people.

Get it on the App Store → · babbel.com

3. Busuu

Best for: getting feedback on what you write and say · Level: A1–B2

Busuu’s lessons follow the European levels from A1 to B2, and its most useful feature is the community: you write or record an answer, and native speakers correct it. Getting real corrections on your own sentences is rare in an app, and it is where I noticed the most progress.

Where it falls short: the quality of corrections varies, and the best features need a subscription.

Get it on the App Store → · busuu.com

Apps for speaking and listening

4. Pimsleur

Best for: speaking out loud and getting your pronunciation right · Level: A1–B1

Pimsleur is audio-based: a speaker prompts you, you answer out loud, and the lessons build in a careful sequence. It is the app that got me speaking earliest, and it is perfect for commutes or walks. The Spanish it teaches is Latin American, which suits most learners in the United States.

Where it falls short: it is expensive, and vocabulary grows slowly. Pair it with reading.

Get it on the App Store → · pimsleur.com

5. Dreaming Spanish

Best for: listening, from the very first day · Level: A1–C1

Dreaming Spanish teaches through comprehensible input: thousands of videos, sorted by level, where native speakers talk about everyday topics using gestures and drawings so that you understand without translation. There are guides from Spain and several Latin American countries. If your listening is your weakest skill, this is the tool I recommend. I explain the idea behind it in {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input for Spanish}}.

Where it falls short: it doesn’t teach grammar explicitly, and progress feels slow at first, which is part of the method.

Get it on the App Store →

6. Language Transfer

Best for: understanding how Spanish works, for free · Level: A1–B1

Language Transfer’s Complete Spanish is a free audio course where the teacher guides a student to build sentences by thinking, not memorizing. It is especially good at showing how English and Spanish connect, and it made many grammar ideas click for me. For a free resource, it is remarkable.

Where it falls short: it is audio only, with a single teacher’s voice, so add other listening.

Get it on the App Store → · languagetransfer.org

{{image:2}}

Apps for vocabulary and reference

7. SpanishDict

Best for: a quick dictionary and full conjugation tables · Level: All levels

SpanishDict is the app I open most, even as a translator. It combines a good dictionary with example sentences, regional notes and complete conjugation tables for every verb. It also has simple grammar guides and quizzes. I review it in more detail with other tools in my list of the {{link:best-spanish-dictionary|best Spanish dictionaries}}.

Where it falls short: it is a reference, not a course.

Get it on the App Store → · spanishdict.com

8. Anki

Best for: remembering words for months, not days · Level: All levels

Anki is a flashcard app that uses spaced repetition: it shows you each card just before you are likely to forget it. It looks plain and takes a weekend to set up well, but it is the most effective vocabulary tool I have used. The trick is to make cards with whole sentences rather than single words, a habit I describe in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.

Where it falls short: the interface is old-fashioned, and the iPhone app is paid.

Get it on the App Store → · free desktop and Android versions

Apps for real conversation

9. italki and Preply

Best for: speaking with a real person, at your level · Level: All levels

No app replaces a conversation with a patient human. On italki and Preply you can book one-on-one lessons with tutors from Mexico, Colombia, Spain and everywhere else, at a time that suits you. Even one 30-minute conversation a week makes everything you learn in other apps usable.

Where it falls short: it costs more per hour than apps, and finding the right tutor can take a few tries. Tip: choose a tutor from the country whose Spanish you want to speak.

Get it on the App Store → · Preply on the App Store

{{image:3}}

How I would combine the best apps to learn Spanish

Your goalCombination
Just starting, on a budgetDuolingo + Language Transfer + SpanishDict
Structured learningBabbel + Anki + one tutor session a week
Speaking for travel or familyPimsleur + a tutor on italki or Preply
Understanding real SpanishDreaming Spanish + podcasts + Anki

Whatever you choose, add some reading: apps rarely give you enough. My list of the {{link:best-books-to-learn-spanish|best books to learn Spanish}} and the {{link:best-spanish-podcasts|best Spanish podcasts}} fill those gaps.

Final thoughts

The best app to learn Spanish is the one you will open tomorrow, and the best plan is a small combination that covers listening, speaking, vocabulary and grammar. Pick two or three apps from this list, use them every day for a month, and adjust from there.

faq.q: What is the best app to learn Spanish?
faq.a: It depends on your goal: Duolingo for habit, Babbel for structure, Pimsleur for speaking, Dreaming Spanish for listening and a tutor app for conversation. Most learners do best combining two or three.

faq.q: What is the best free app to learn Spanish?
faq.a: Duolingo and Language Transfer are excellent free options, and SpanishDict and Anki are free references and tools.

faq.q: Can you become fluent with apps alone?
faq.a: Rarely. Apps build habits and knowledge, but you also need real reading, listening and conversation with people.

faq.q: Which Spanish app is best for speaking?
faq.a: Pimsleur for guided speaking practice, and italki or Preply for real conversation with a tutor.

faq.q: Do these apps teach Latin American or Spain Spanish?
faq.a: Most default to Latin American Spanish. Dreaming Spanish and tutor platforms let you choose speakers from specific countries.
